cards.body:
A sequence of n appends to a geometrically growing array costs O(n) time in total.

cards.title: Invariant: Dynamic array append is amortized O(1)
cards.body: After every append, capacity is at least length; immediately after a resize, capacity is at most twice length.

cards.title: Proof step: Base case
cards.body: The first append writes one slot into the initial capacity and performs no copy.

cards.title: Proof step: Resize points form a geometric series
cards.body:
Capacity doubles only when length reaches capacity, so resizes happen at lengths 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on.

Depends on: base

cards.title: Proof step: Total copy work is bounded

Across all resizes the array copies at most 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n slots, which is less than 2n.

Depends on: doubling

n appends perform n writes and fewer than 2n copies, so the sequence is linear and each append is O(1) on average.

cards.title: Invariant: Bottom-up heapify is linear
cards.body: Before node i is processed, every subtree rooted at an index greater than i is already a valid heap.

cards.title: Proof step: Leaves are heaps
cards.body: Nodes with no children already satisfy the heap property, so processing can start at the last parent.

cards.title: Proof step: Process internal nodes bottom-up
cards.body:

Depends on: leaves

cards.title: Proof step: Cost depends on height
cards.body:
A node at height h moves at most h levels, and a binary heap has at most ceil(n / 2^(h+1)) nodes at height h.

Depends on: reverse

cards.title: Proof step: Bound the weighted sum
cards.body:
The sum over heights of h * n / 2^(h+1) is at most n, because the series sum h / 2^h converges to 2.

cards.title: Invariant: Sliding window moves each pointer at most n times
cards.body: At the start of every iteration the half-open interval [left, right) is the current window and right is one past the last inspected element.

D. It disables database commits entirely

**A.** A test's writes are wrapped in a transaction that rolls back, leaving the database clean. No explicit cleanup needed; the database is fresh for the next test.

cards.title: Q4: What is a contract test?

A. A test that verifies a service conforms to its API contract (request/response format)
B. A test that always passes
C. A test that uses mocking instead of real services
D. A test that runs only on Sundays

**A.** Contract tests verify that both client and server agree on API format (schema, status codes, error messages). Misalignment breaks the contract.

cards.title: Q5: Why might you use a module-scoped fixture instead of a sessi

A. Module scope runs faster because it reuses setup across more tests
B. Module scope provides finer isolation granularity; setup is shared per module, not per session
C. Module scope is always slower and should be avoided
D. Module scope disables cleanup

**B.** Module scope balances speed (reuse setup per module) and isolation (fresh setup for each new module). It's a middle ground between function and session scopes.

**B.** Pytest uses the test function's parameter names to match fixtures. If a test has a parameter named 'tmp_path', Pytest injects the built-in tmp_path fixture.

B. A pytest file that defines shared fixtures available to all tests in that directory and subdirectories
C. A test file that runs configuration checks

**B.** conftest.py is a pytest convention; fixtures defined there are automatically discovered and available to all tests in that directory and subdirectories.

cards.title: Q3: How does the `yield` keyword in a fixture work?
cards.body:
A. It skips the test if the condition is false
B. It returns a value from the fixture
C. It separates setup (before yield) from cleanup (after yield)
D. It makes the fixture run in parallel

**C.** yield separates setup and cleanup in a fixture. Code before yield runs before the test; code after yield runs after the test, even if the test fails.

cards.title: Q4: What does fixture scope control?
cards.body:
A. Whether the fixture is visible in other test files
B. When setup runs and when cleanup happens (function, module, session)
C. How many tests can use the fixture
D. The order in which tests run

**B.** Fixture scope determines: function-scoped fixtures run before each test; module-scoped fixtures run once per module; session-scoped fixtures run once per session.

**C.** A fixture can take another fixture as a parameter. Pytest resolves the dependency chain and runs setup in order.
